hindu-arabic.supports: The digits originated in India (6th or 7th century) and reached Europe through Middle Eastern mathematicians such as al-Khwarizmi. The Hindus were the first to use zero in the modern way.
hindu-arabic.checked: Search-result summary of the page (the page itself could not be opened).

roman-no-zero.ref: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Is It Still Important to Learn Roman Numerals?'
roman-no-zero.supports: Zero cannot be written with Roman numerals.
roman-no-zero.checked: Search-result summary of the page (the page itself could not be opened).

egyptian.supports: Separate symbols for 1, 10, 100, 1000 and so on, each repeated as often as needed (an additive system with no place value); 1000 is a lotus flower. Wording approved by Dion 2026-10-03: 'Egyptian numerals had no place value, so they did not need a zero digit to hold empty places.'
egyptian.checked: Search-result summary of the page (the page itself could not be opened).

babylonian.ref: Any reliable history-of-mathematics source on the Babylonian sexagesimal (base-60) system, e.g. Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Cuneiform numeral'
babylonian.supports: The Babylonians used a base-60 (sexagesimal) system, which is the origin of 60 minutes in an hour and 60 seconds in a minute.
babylonian.checked: Fact approved by Dion 2026-10-03 (TR-D02): any reliable history-of-mathematics source is acceptable; no specific article is required.

tally.supports: One mark is made for each object counted, so there is no mark for zero.

number-roles.ref: Standard school definitions of cardinal, ordinal and nominal numbers
number-roles.supports: Cardinal: how many. Ordinal: position or order. Nominal: a label that does not count anything (phone, taxi or shirt number).
number-roles.checked: Not externally sourced: compare with the pupil's textbook.

line-notation.ref: Notation used in Cameroonian Form 1 mathematics (French-influenced): (AB) line, [AB) half line, [AB] segment, AB length
line-notation.supports: Which brackets name which figure; a half line is named from its end point; a line has no end point and no length.
line-notation.checked: Not externally sourced: compare with the pupil's exercise book.

one-line-two-points.ref: Euclid, Elements, Book I, Postulate 1 (a straight line can be drawn between any two points)
one-line-two-points.supports: Exactly one straight line passes through two different points, so any two points are collinear; three points need not be.

midpoint.ref: Definition of the midpoint of a segment; the perpendicular bisector as the set of points equidistant from A and B
midpoint.supports: MA = MB alone does not make M the midpoint: every point of the perpendicular bisector has MA = MB, and only the one on [AB] is the midpoint.

perpendicular-bisector.ref: Euclid, Elements, Book I, Proposition 10 (bisecting a segment); the standard ruler-and-compasses construction of the perpendicular bisector
perpendicular-bisector.supports: The construction steps and their order; the bisector passes through the midpoint at a right angle and not through A; its points are equidistant from A and B.

parallel-postulate.ref: Playfair's axiom (equivalent to Euclid's parallel postulate); Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Euclidean geometry'
parallel-postulate.supports: Through a point not on a line there is exactly one parallel line.
parallel-postulate.checked: Search-result summary of the page (the page itself could not be opened).

one-perpendicular.ref: Euclid, Elements, Book I, Proposition 12, and the standard uniqueness theorem for perpendiculars in a plane
one-perpendicular.supports: Through a point not on a line there is exactly one line perpendicular to it.

line-symbols.ref: Symbols // (parallel) and ⊥ (perpendicular) as used in Form 1
line-symbols.supports: // means parallel (never meet); ⊥ means perpendicular (meet at a right angle).
line-symbols.checked: Not externally sourced: compare with the pupil's exercise book.
